name: Vulvectomy
overview: Surgical removal of vulvar tissue for malignancy

pimpingQuestions.question: The vulva develops from the genital tubercle and labioscrotal folds. What are the homologous structures in male and female external genitalia?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Genital tubercle → clitoris (female) / glans penis (male). Urethral folds → labia minora / ventral penile shaft. Labioscrotal swellings → labia majora / scrotum. The vestibular bulbs (female) are homologous to the corpus spongiosum (male). Understanding these homologies matters because vulvar carcinoma SCC arises predominantly from keratinized squamous epithelium of the labia majora — the same tissue type as penile SCC.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the inguinofemoral lymph node anatomy critical to radical vulvectomy, and what is Cloquet's node?
pimpingQuestions.answer: The superficial inguinal nodes (8-10 nodes above the cribriform fascia) receive primary vulvar lymphatic drainage. Deep inguinal nodes (3-5 nodes medial to the femoral vein, below the cribriform fascia) include Cloquet's node (the most cephalad deep inguinal node, at the femoral ring). Cloquet's node is the sentinel to pelvic node involvement — if negative on frozen section, pelvic lymphadenectomy can be omitted (Hacker's principle).

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the blood supply to the vulva, and which vessel's injury causes the most significant bleeding during vulvectomy?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Internal pudendal artery (main supply — branches: perineal artery, posterior labial arteries, artery of the vestibular bulb, dorsal artery of the clitoris). External pudendal arteries (from femoral — supply labia majora). The pudendal artery branches within the ischioanal fossa (Alcock's canal). The artery of the vestibular bulb is the most commonly injured vessel during vulvectomy — the bulb is an erectile vascular structure that can cause significant hemorrhage if not controlled.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the most significant complication after radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Wound breakdown/dehiscence (30-60%) — the highest wound complication rate of any oncologic procedure. This is because the groin incisions overlie a mobile, moist, bacteria-rich area with poor vascularity after node dissection. The triple-incision technique (separate vulvar and bilateral groin incisions via skin bridges) reduced wound breakdown from 60-80% (en bloc 'butterfly' incision) to 30-40%. Chronic lymphedema of the lower extremities occurs in 30-50%.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the role of sentinel lymph node biopsy in vulvar cancer, and what does the GROINSS-V study show?
pimpingQuestions.answer: GROINSS-V (2008) and GROINSS-VI (2016): for unifocal vulvar SCC <4cm, sentinel lymph node biopsy with ultrastaging (serial sections + immunohistochemistry) safely replaces complete inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy when the SLN is negative. Groin recurrence rate with negative SLN: 2.3% (comparable to full dissection). SLN biopsy reduces lymphedema from 25-30% to 2%, and wound complications from 30-40% to 12%. This is now the standard for early-stage vulvar cancer.
